ety.text: From Middle English inland, inlond, from Old English inland, equivalent to in- + land. Compare West Frisian ynlân (“inland”), German Inland (“inland”), Danish indland (“inland”), Swedish inland (“inland”), Norwegian innland (“inland”). Compare also Dutch binnenland.

senses.d: Within the land; relatively remote from the ocean or from open water; interior.
ex: In this wide Inland ſea, that hight by name / The Idle lake, my wandring ſhip I row, […]

senses.d: Limited to the land, or to inland routes; not passing on, or over, the sea.
Confined to one country or state; domestic; not foreign.
Of a sophisticated background, especially as relates to a royal court or national capital.
The interior part of a country.
ex:
a wall sufficient to defend
Our inland from the pilfering borderers.

senses.d: Into, or towards, the interior of the land, away from the coast.
ex: The greatest waves of population have rolled inland from the east.
